title: Find Pivot Index
description: Find the first index where the sum of earlier elements equals the sum of later elements. Exclude the element at the index from both sums. Return -1 when no such index exists.
constraints: Values may be negative, zero, or positive.
hints: Can one total sum help you avoid summing both sides at every index?
Keep a running left sum. The right sum is total − left − current.
Check the equality before adding the current element to the left sum.
steps: Compute the total once.
Scan left to right, comparing left with total − left − current.
Return the first matching index, or -1 after the scan.
complexityExplanation: Two linear scans take O(n) time. Only total, left and the index are retained, so auxiliary space is O(1).

title: Maximum Subarray
description: Return the greatest sum among all nonempty contiguous subarrays. A subarray keeps the original order and contains consecutive elements.
constraints: The chosen subarray must contain at least one element.

examples.note: All-negative arrays still need a nonempty result.
One element is a valid subarray.

hints: At each position, should you extend the previous subarray or start a new one?
Track the best sum ending here separately from the best sum anywhere.
Initialize both sums with the first element; starting at zero breaks all-negative cases.
steps: Initialize ending and best with the first element.
Update ending = max(current, ending + current).
Update best at every position and return it.
complexityExplanation: Each element is processed once. The solution uses two running sums, with no sliced copy of the input.

title: BFS Shortest Path
description: Given an unweighted graph, return one shortest path from start to goal. Return an empty list if the goal is unreachable. Vertices are numbered 0 through V − 1. Use an adjacency list in Python and the supplied adjacency matrix in C.
constraints: Edges may be directed. A start equal to the goal has path [start].
hints: In an unweighted graph, which traversal visits vertices by increasing distance?
Store the predecessor of each vertex when it first enters the queue.
Walk backward from goal through predecessors, then reverse the path.
steps: Mark start visited and enqueue it.
Process neighbors in queue order; record each first predecessor.
If goal was reached, reconstruct its predecessor chain.
complexityExplanation: Python scans each adjacency-list edge once: O(V + E). The C matrix version scans V possible neighbors per visited vertex: O(V²). Both use O(V) auxiliary space for the queue and predecessors. Input graph storage and returned path are excluded.

title: Course Schedule II
description: Courses are numbered 0 through V − 1. Each prerequisite pair [course, prerequisite] requires the second course to come first. Return any valid order of all courses. Return an empty list when dependencies contain a cycle.
constraints: Prerequisite pairs are unique and use valid course IDs.
No pair uses the same course twice.

examples.note: The dependency cycle prevents a full order.
A course without prerequisites is ready.

hints: Which courses are available before completing any other course?
Track the number of unmet prerequisites (indegree) and queue all zero-indegree courses.
After taking a course, reduce its dependents’ indegrees. Fewer than V processed courses indicates a cycle.
steps: Build edges from prerequisite to course and count indegrees.
Queue all courses with indegree zero.
Process each edge once; accept the order only if it contains every course.

solutions.python:
from collections import deque

def course_order(V, prerequisites):
    graph = [[] for _ in range(V)]
    indegree = [0] * V
    for course, prerequisite in prerequisites:
        graph[prerequisite].append(course)
        indegree[course] += 1
    queue = deque(i for i in range(V) if indegree[i] == 0)
    order = []
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        order.append(node)
        for neighbor in graph[node]:
            indegree[neighbor] -= 1
            if indegree[neighbor] == 0:
                queue.append(neighbor)
    return order if len(order) == V else []

complexityExplanation: Building and processing the adjacency list takes O(V + E) time and space, including the internally built graph. The input pairs and returned order are excluded.

title: Binary Tree Traversals
description: Return the preorder, inorder, and postorder sequences of a binary tree. Preorder visits root, left, right; inorder visits left, root, right; postorder visits left, right, root. An empty tree produces three empty sequences.
constraints: Height ≤ 200 for these recursive reference implementations.
Python uses Node(val, left, right). C uses struct Node.

examples.note: Move the root visit to change traversal order.

hints: Each order traverses the same tree. Only the position of the root visit changes.
Use one recursive walk with a visit before left, between children, and after right.
Always stop when the node is None or NULL.
steps: Stop at empty children.
Append before left recursion for preorder and between recursions for inorder.
Append after right recursion for postorder.
complexityExplanation: Every node is visited once. Recursion uses O(h) auxiliary space, where h is the tree height. The three returned sequences use O(n) output space, excluded from this check.

title: Maximum Depth of a Binary Tree
description: Return the number of nodes on the longest path from the root to a leaf. An empty tree has depth 0; a single node has depth 1.
constraints: Height ≤ 200 for the recursive reference implementations.
Missing children are None in Python and NULL in C.

examples.note: The longest root-to-leaf path contains 3 nodes.

hints: How does a tree’s depth relate to the depths of its two subtrees?
An empty subtree contributes zero.
For any real node, return 1 + max(left depth, right depth).
steps: Return 0 for an empty root.
Recursively compute both child depths.
Return one plus the greater depth.
complexityExplanation: Each node contributes one recursive call, giving O(n) time. Simultaneous calls are bounded by the height h: O(h) auxiliary stack space, or O(n) in a skewed tree.

title: Coin Change II
description: Count combinations of unique positive coin denominations that sum to amount. Each denomination is available without limit. Different orders of the same coins count as one combination. Return 0 if the amount cannot be formed.
constraints: Coin values are positive and distinct.
The final answer fits a signed 32-bit integer.

examples.note: Only even amounts can be formed.

hints: Let dp[s] count combinations for amount s. What should dp[0] be?
Put the coin loop outside the amount loop to avoid counting orderings.
For each coin, scan amounts upward and add dp[s − coin] to dp[s].
steps: Set dp[0] = 1 and all other counts to zero.
For each coin, update amounts from coin through amount.
Return dp[amount].
complexityExplanation: With k coin denominations and target amount A, the nested loops take O(k × A) time and the DP array takes O(A) space. This treats arithmetic as constant cost; Python uses arbitrary-precision counts.

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
description: Decide whether a nonempty array of positive integers can be split into two groups with equal sums. Each element must belong to exactly one group.
constraints: Each element may be selected at most once.

examples.note: An odd total cannot be split equally.
An even total alone is insufficient.

hints: If the total sum is odd, can two equal integer sums exist?
Reduce the task to finding a subset with half the total sum.
Scan target sums downward so an element cannot be reused in the same iteration.
steps: Reject an odd total and set target to half the total.
Use a boolean DP array with dp[0] = true.
For each value, update sums downward; return dp[target].
complexityExplanation: Let S be half the total sum. The algorithm takes O(n × S) time and O(S) auxiliary space. This is pseudo-polynomial, since it depends on numeric values.

title: Binary Search
description: Find target in a strictly increasing integer array. Return its zero-based index, or -1 when absent. Solve it without scanning every element.
constraints: All elements are distinct and sorted ascending.
Target may lie outside the array’s range.
hints: A comparison with the middle value rules out half the remaining positions.
Use inclusive bounds lo and hi. Continue while lo ≤ hi.
Discard mid itself with lo = mid + 1 or hi = mid − 1 to guarantee progress.
steps: Initialize bounds to the first and last indices.
Compare the middle value with target and keep only the appropriate half.
Return -1 when the interval is empty.
complexityExplanation: The interval halves after every comparison, so worst-case time is O(log n). The iterative version retains only bounds and a midpoint.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
description: A strictly increasing array of distinct integers has been rotated by an unknown offset, possibly zero. Find target and return its index, or -1 when absent. Aim for logarithmic time.
constraints: The input is a rotation of an ascending array.

examples.note: The target is in the rotated right segment.

hints: At least one half around the midpoint is sorted when values are distinct.
Check nums[lo] ≤ nums[mid] to identify a sorted left half.
Keep a sorted half only when target lies within its bounds; otherwise keep the other half.
steps: Check the midpoint for a match.
Identify which half is sorted.
Use that half’s value bounds to discard half the interval.
complexityExplanation: Distinct values let each iteration discard half the interval: O(log n) worst-case time. The iterative implementation uses O(1) auxiliary space. With duplicate values this bound would not be guaranteed.
